set.longDescription:
Once the first missionary generation had passed, Catholicism in Spanish America settled into being the ordinary religion of whole societies, and its real institutions were local: the cofradías, lay confraternities that maintained an altar or an image, buried their members and paid for their funerals, organized by trade, by parish and often by race — with indigenous confraternities and Black brotherhoods running their own devotional life. Its saints were homegrown: Rose of Lima, canonized in 1671 as the first saint of the Americas, and Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of the same city. Its convents produced writers of the first rank, among them Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz in Mexico, who defended a woman's right to study, and Úrsula de Jesús in Lima, an enslaved woman later freed, whose spiritual diary survives in her own dictated words. Above all it produced Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose shrine at Tepeyac became the devotional center of Mexico and eventually a symbol of Mexican identity itself.

Portuguese America had its own brotherhoods. In Bahia a sermon of 1633 is headed as preached to the brotherhood of the Blacks of a sugar mill, on the feast of St John the Evangelist. It is by the Jesuit António Vieira, in his Maria Rosa Mystica of 1686. In the same book he tells the enslaved workers of a sugar mill that no labor in the world is more like the Cross and Passion of Christ than theirs (a rendering). In 1711 André João Antonil wrote of the mills. He says some masters keep enslaved people for a long time in the cane fields or the mill without baptism. He tells masters not to object when the enslaved choose their own kings. He tells them to let the enslaved keep their morning feasts of Our Lady of the Rosary, of St Benedict and of the patron of the mill chapel. In 1741 Benedict XIV wrote to the bishops of Brazil, Paraguay and the Río de la Plata. His bull Immensa pastorum principis condemned those who enslaved or sold Indians, even baptized ones.

Saint-Domingue, the French colony that became Haiti, is seen here through one long witness. It is the Description of Moreau de Saint-Méry, printed in Philadelphia in 1797. It shows the colony as it stood on 18 October 1789. Moreau was at Le Cap in 1783, and in 1788 the Navy minister gave him a drafting task for the colonies. He writes from the colonists' side, so the picture of the Black people in it is his, not theirs.

He says the parishes of the North first had Capuchins as pastors. In 1704 the Capuchins could not supply enough men and gave up the mission. The Jesuits took it over and kept it until their order was expelled from the colony, at the end of 1763. Secular priests held it until 1768, when the Capuchins came back. In the West, the Dominicans served the parishes.

Moreau judges the Africans of the colony harshly. He says they could not sort religious ideas in their minds, so that all their belief lay in outward signs. In church, he says, they mumbled prayers they knew badly, or slept. Yet he reports that new arrivals from Africa pressed to be baptized. Black people born in the colony claimed to stand far above them because of their baptism, and the newcomers were taunted as "horses". Adults were baptized on two Saturdays of the year, often with no preparation. He says they held a godparent in more respect than their own father and mother.

At Le Cap, after the parish Mass on Sundays, Black worshippers met in the church. They prayed and sang hymns, led by some old men and women. A low Mass followed, which Moreau calls la messe des nègres, the Mass of the Black people. He credits the Jesuit Pierre Boutin, who reached Le Cap in 1705, with teaching them each evening, with the baptism of adults at Easter and Pentecost, and with that Mass.

Guatemala gave this world a brotherhood that ran a hospital. It was called the Bethlemites. Pedro de Betancur founded it and took the name Pedro de San José.

Two books tell his story, and both are hagiography, written to honor him. One is a Life printed at Rome in 1683, by Francisco Antonio de Montalvo. The other is the order's own history of 1723, by Joseph García de la Concepción, a Discalced Franciscan who wrote it for the order.

Montalvo says Pedro was born on Tenerife. He sailed for the Indies in 1650 and reached Guatemala City in 1651. He died in April 1667.

Montalvo writes of the Hospital of Our Lady of Bethlehem. He also writes of a Bethlemite Company that Pedro was to found. It was to shelter the sick, the poor and the abandoned. Members of the Third Order of St Francis, he says, moved over to the new house of hospitality.

Montalvo's Life is full of wonders. In one, he says, the Virgin let Pedro know how welcome his service was, by a favor no less rare than miraculous. Of one such wonder Montalvo says he offers it only as human report, because the Sacred Congregation of Rites is the body that weighs miracles.

García says the brothers sent their constitutions to Brother Antonio de la Cruz at Madrid. He was to go to Rome and seek apostolic confirmation. Antonio went to the Roman Curia and won papal confirmation of the constitutions. García prints the bull of Clement X for it.

García also prints a bull of Innocent XI. It closes with the date 26 March 1687, in the eleventh year of that pope's reign. A later memorial recalls the pope's grace in raising the Company to a regular community under the Rule of St Augustine.

sources.work: The cofradia books: confraternity records across New Spain and Peru, incl. indigenous confraternities' books and Black brotherhoods' records (Afro-Peruvian and Afro-Brazilian rosary confraternities)
sources.note: A lay-run devotional economy that was the ordinary institutional life of the piety; the records themselves were kept under clerical oversight.

sources.work: Convent writings, women's: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea (1691; trans. Arenal & Powell); Madre Maria de San Jose's autobiography (ed. Myers & Powell); Ursula de Jesus, The Souls of Purgatory (ed./trans. van Deusen, UNM, 2004)
sources.note: An enslaved-then-freed convent servant's dictated spiritual diary, begun in 1650 - an enslaved woman's own religious voice, though filtered through the confessor who took her dictation. The convent's racial hierarchy is visible within it.

sources.work: The canonization processes: Rose of Lima (canonized 1671), Martin de Porres (process testimony from the 1660s, ordinary witnesses incl. Afro-Peruvians), Mariana de Quito
sources.note: Canonization-process testimony is structured and led by the questioners, but it remains the era's densest record of ordinary devotees speaking for themselves.

sources.work: The devotional-practice layer: the Guadalupan corpus (Nican Mopohua, published 1649 in Huei tlamahuicoltica; its dating and authorship are still debated), shrine and pilgrimage records, novena imprints; Inquisition and extirpation records that policed popular devotion
sources.note: The records that policed popular devotion come from a hostile administrative source.

sources.work: William B. Taylor, Magistrates of the Sacred (Stanford, 1996), with Asuncion Lavrin, Brides of Christ (Stanford, 2008)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, ch. 19 'Christianity in Iberian America' (Riley)
sources.note: A direct fit for this movement, with the chapter number confirmed.

sources.work: António Vieira, Maria Rosa Mystica (Lisbon: Miguel Deslandes, 1686)
sources.note: Thirty sermons on the Rosary. Sermon XIV is headed as preached in Bahia to the Blacks' brotherhood of a sugar mill. Read in full text online. The print is noisy (the long s) and its wording should be checked against the page images.

sources.note: A long description of the French colony as it stood in 1789. It is a colonial author's view of the Black people it describes, and no enslaved voice speaks in the passages read. Held in the Library; the print is noisy (the long s reads as f).

sources.work: Francisco Antonio de Montalvo, Vida admirable y muerte preciosa del venerable hermano Pedro de S. Joseph Betancur, fundador de la Compañía Bethlemitica en las Yndias Occidentales (Rome: Nicolas Angel Tinassi, 1683)

set.longDescription:
Before the Civil War most Black Christians in America worshipped under white supervision. And made something else of it anyway, in praise houses, brush arbors and night meetings where the preaching, the singing and the theology were their own. Independent congregations appear from the 1770s (Silver Bluff in South Carolina, First African Baptist in Savannah in 1788), and in 1816 Richard Allen, who had walked out of a Philadelphia Methodist church with the rest of its Black members after a trustee pulled Absalom Jones up off his knees in the segregated gallery, organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church — the first Black denomination of national reach; AME Zion followed in 1821. Because the law in much of the South forbade the enslaved to read, the tradition's theology comes down to us largely in what it sang and told: the spirituals, conversion accounts, and self-published narratives like Jarena Lee's. By 1906 it was a whole world of its own. Denominations, colleges, newspapers and a worship life that was about to reshape global Christianity from a mission on Azusa Street.

In 1874 a church in the United States made a bishop for Haiti, and its mission board asked that he be of the African race. The Spirit of Missions for December 1874, the journal of the Protestant Episcopal Church's mission board, prints a triennial report on the Haitian church. It is signed by J. Theodore Holly as Dean, at Port-au-Prince on 30 June 1874, but Holly's own part is a table of districts and his signature. The story around it is the board's.

The board also wanted him to be a Haitian citizen. The Dean of the Haitian Convocation came to make a covenant with the American church. By it, the Church in Haiti was a foreign church, still aided by the American one.

The Haitian church promised to keep the doctrine, worship and discipline of the American church. The House of Bishops chose Holly as the first bishop. He was consecrated in Grace Church, New York, on 8 November 1874.

sources.work: Richard Allen, The Life Experience and Gospel Labors (pub. 1833); the 1794 yellow-fever vindication pamphlet (with Absalom Jones); AME Doctrines and Discipline (1817) and General Conference minutes; Daniel Coker, A Dialogue between a Virginian and an African Minister (1810)
sources.note: The founding bishop's own narrative and the church's own records from the start.

sources.work: Jarena Lee, The Life and Religious Experience of Jarena Lee (1836; expanded 1849); Zilpha Elaw, Memoirs (1846); Julia Foote, A Brand Plucked from the Fire (1879)
sources.note: Black women preachers' own narratives (Lee self-published, with Allen's authorization recorded in her own words), collected in Andrews's Sisters of the Spirit.

sources.work: Slave narratives as primary religious texts: Douglass, Narrative (1845, with the appendix on slaveholding religion); Sojourner Truth, Narrative (1850 - dictated); God Struck Me Dead (Fisk interviews, 1920s); WPA ex-slave narratives (1930s)
sources.note: These narratives carry real editorial filters: abolitionist framing, dictation rather than self-authorship in some cases, and interviewer bias. The Fisk and WPA interviews were recorded in the 1920s and 1930s, decades after the events they describe.

sources.work: Spirituals as communal theology: Slave Songs of the United States (1867) and the Fisk Jubilee Singers' repertoire; with David Walker, Appeal (1829) and The Confessions of Nat Turner (1831, recorded by Thomas R. Gray)
sources.note: The spirituals survive here through white transcription and concert-stage arrangement, both real filters on the original oral form. Walker's Appeal is a direct work of Black prophetic writing. Turner's Confessions were recorded by Thomas R. Gray, a white lawyer, from a captive man facing execution - a hostile and coercive context for the text.

sources.work: Albert J. Raboteau, Slave Religion (OUP, 1978; updated 2004), with Milton Sernett (ed.), African American Religious History: A Documentary Witness (Duke, 2nd ed. 1999)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated chapter on the Black church; chapter 35 (Kalu) touches on the Atlantic diaspora as related context.

sources.work: The Spirit of Missions, vol. 39 (December 1874): the Triennial Report of the Missionary Jurisdiction of Haiti for 1872-74, signed by J. Theodore Holly as Dean, and the Board's account of the Haitien Episcopate
sources.note: Holly's own part is a table and his signature; the narrative is the Mission Board's, an American Episcopal view of the Haitian church. Held in the Library.

neighbor_changes.ruling: G89-18 a: G89c, source now held
neighbor_changes.reason: LA8-6 names Holly as a named line in VIII.1 or VIII.46. VIII.1 is chosen (c. 1770s-1906); the report of December 1874 sits inside it. Only what the report says is drafted; the 1861 emigration is held.

holds.item: LA8-6: the Catholic church of Haiti after 1860 (the concordat church)
holds.reason: No French or Haitian Catholic source in the Library. The 1860 Concordat printing was not found. VIII.46 is unchanged (no end moved to 1906).
holds.waits_for: A pre-1930 source on the concordat church: the Concordat text of 28 March 1860, or a French account of the clergy sent after it.

holds.item: LA8-6: Holly's emigration of 1861 and his early work
holds.reason: The December 1874 issue does not mention 1861, Holly's birthplace or the emigrants. The report's table of districts is too noisy to quote.
holds.waits_for: Holly's own writings or a pre-1930 source on the 1861 emigration to Haiti.

holds.item: LA8-6: the Code Noir (1685), the religious side of the rising of 1791 (Bois Caïman)
holds.reason: Moreau's Description (read for the church passages) gave no Bois Caïman passage on a search of tome I. The Code Noir was not read.
holds.waits_for: A source that states them (the Code Noir text; a pre-1930 account of 1791).

holds.item: LA8-9: the Bethlemites after 1723, their end in 1820, the order's spread outside Guatemala, and the approvals of 1707 and later
holds.reason: García's OCR is damaged in the later books; only clean lines are used.
holds.waits_for: A clean reading of García's third book and a source for 1820; Clement XI's bulls of 1707 (not read).

holds.reason: Claret's Apuntes (1863) is a rule for governing a diocese. It shows him as archbishop of Santiago de Cuba, called to Madrid by the Queen, with Havana and Puerto Rico as suffragans, but says nothing of the church under the crown's patronage, of Puerto Rico's church or of the end of Spanish rule in 1898, the line the gate names. A partial line on Claret alone is possible but is not the gate's line; held for the coordinator.
holds.waits_for: a dated source on the church in Cuba under Spanish rule, 1815-1898 (for example Claret's own letters from Santiago, or a diocesan report)

wants: A French Catholic source for Haiti 1860-1906
A pre-1930 source on Holly's emigration of 1861
flags: OCR: Moreau tome I line 6894 reads 'T763' for 1763 (the year is confirmed by the header's content note and by line 19252, 'En 1764, on vit arriver l'abbé de la Roque'). Moreau line 2612 reads 'xle' for 'de' and 'oij' for 'où'. Line 18653 reads 'raeffe' for 'messe'.

OCR: Montalvo and García use the long s as f throughout and have other damaged letters (quoted verbatim). García line 40982 reads 'i62y' for the year of the bull of Innocent XI; the year 1687 is read from the page image (leaf n456), as the review confirmed, and matches the sweep record.

'First order founded in the Americas' (sweep record) is not drafted: neither Montalvo nor García states it in the lines read. The titles give 'fundador de la Compañía Bethlemitica en las Yndias Occidentales'.

Clement X's bull is named but not dated: the lines read give no year. García prints another Clement X bull dated at line 32148-32151 (5 December of a year read 'i<í74>', year 5 of his reign), but it is not clear that it is the confirming bull, so it is not used.
'James' in Holly's name and 1861 are the sweep record's, not the issue's. The draft says only 'J. Theodore Holly' and nothing of 1861; the emigration stays a hold.

Moreau 'a white colonist': the Description does not say so in the passages read. The draft says he writes from the colonists' side (a reading of his tone) and records the two things the text shows, that he was at Le Cap in 1783 and was commissioned by the Navy minister in 1788. The coordinator's word 'lawyer' is not in the title page.

Countries: not added anywhere. VII.17's place label is 'Peru · Brazil and beyond' (the validator allows at most two places drawn from the region text, which reads 'New Spain, Peru, Brazil'), so Haiti (Q790, from VIII.46) and Guatemala cannot go on VII.17. VIII.48's place label is 'Spanish America · Brazil' (region 'Spanish America, Brazil'), so Cuba cannot go on it. VIII.1's place label is 'United States', one place, region 'United States', so Haiti cannot go on it without a region change that no ruling names. No country IDs were invented.

No link drafted. Holly's issue names the Catholic church of Haiti nowhere (the one 'Roman Catholic' in it, line 5099, is about women's work). Buteau is called 'substantially heathen' by the Board (line 2981); it is not used.
No frozen paragraph was changed. The existing paragraphs of VII.17, VIII.1 and VIII.48 are carried unchanged; the checker may print readability lines for them (that is not new text).
Moreau, Montalvo, García and Claret add no people rows: no row is new, and the existing people lists are left as they are. Pierre Boutin and Brother Antonio are named only inside the prose.
